technology_signal_gate.summary: The assessment identifies a material 2026 delta across labour-market entry effects, software valuation/pricing, infrastructure capital intensity and competition evidence; it provides a scale path, transmission mechanisms, contrary evidence and explicit falsifiers rather than a generic technology roundup.

factual_methodology.summary: Quantitative claims are traceable to Stanford HAI and Digital Economy Lab, ILO, OECD, NBER, METR, IEA, SEG, Stripe, Salesforce, FTC, European Commission and Microsoft's 10-K. Investor views from Thiel, Sequoia, Bessemer, a16z and SoftBank are explicitly labelled as theses or expectations rather than empirical findings.

taxonomy.summary: Program, three dimensions, global geography, controlled topics and phenomena, assessment format and weekly cadence match taxonomy v1.0 and the weekly technology-signal contract.

translation_semantics.summary: EN and PT-BR preserve the same thesis, numerical values, qualifications, contrary evidence, scenarios, falsifiers and visual sequence. Technical terms retained in PT-BR are used where they are established market terminology or named product concepts.

editorial_publication_readiness.summary: The opening states a falsifiable thesis; sections move from capital and physical constraints through labour, software economics, concentration, investor lenses and social distribution; the text avoids deterministic job-loss and SaaS-collapse claims.

contextual_depth.summary: The assessment integrates employment pipelines, gender and income exposure, apprenticeship, bargaining power, education, emerging-market dependence, energy systems, local social acceptance, competition policy, capital allocation and 2026–2030 conditional scenarios.

visual_evidence_readiness.signature: 3 explicit bar charts + 4 evidence/scenario tables + 1 flow + 1 mindmap + 1 diagram in each locale
visual_evidence_readiness.summary: Both locales have matching visual structure. Chart values reproduce Stanford private AI investment, IEA data-centre electricity demand and SEG SaaS EV/revenue evidence; structural visuals describe defended mechanisms rather than fabricated quantitative relationships.
visual_evidence_readiness.limitations: The investment chart covers private investment and does not represent total state-backed AI financing; the 2030 electricity value is an IEA projection; the SEG chart is a two-point valuation comparison rather than a causal time series.

contrary_evidence: Stanford payroll evidence does not show widespread economy-wide AI job displacement.
Stripe reports strong SaaS platform formation and higher SaaS payment volumes despite public software valuation compression.
NBER and METR demonstrate that productivity effects vary materially by worker experience, task, tool and research design.
Regulatory scrutiny and concentration indicators do not establish that Big Tech firms constitute an illegal monopoly.
limitations: The 19% young-worker employment gap is US evidence from exposed occupations and should not be generalized mechanically to all countries or jobs.
ILO and OECD exposure measures identify task compatibility with AI, not probabilities of job elimination.
SEG and Stripe data cover their respective company and platform samples rather than the entire global software economy.
Investor theses are included to map capital expectations and value-capture logic; they are not used as independent proof of future market structure.
Scenarios for 2026–2030 are conditional mechanisms without assigned probabilities.
notes: QA approved for public materialization. The article deliberately frames 'monopoly' as an investor/economic lens and uses regulator language such as concentration, gatekeeper and potential competition effects for current market claims.

en.title: AI is making software and cognitive work more abundant — while concentrating the infrastructure that produces them
en.deck: Falling task and application costs are compressing entry-level work and generic software rents while compute, energy, data, distribution and trusted workflows become scarcer and more strategic.
en.regime: AI is lowering the cost of digital production faster than the physical and institutional inputs required to deploy it at scale.
en.key_risk: Productivity gains may coexist with weaker entry-level career ladders and a larger share of economic rents accruing to infrastructure, distribution and capital owners.
watch: SaaS revenue multiples and pricing models

signal_rationale.delta: By October 2026, evidence from labour markets, software valuations, pricing models, cloud regulation and energy infrastructure can be connected into one observable shift: AI is reducing the scarcity of some cognitive tasks and application features while raising the strategic scarcity of compute, power, capital, distribution and trusted workflows.
signal_rationale.evidence: The assessment triangulates Stanford labour and investment data, ILO and OECD occupational exposure, NBER and METR productivity evidence, SEG and Stripe software-market data, Salesforce pricing, IEA physical-infrastructure data, FTC and European Commission competition work, Microsoft filings and clearly labelled investor theses.
signal_rationale.scale_path: Further diffusion depends on lower model and inference costs, reliable agentic workflows and organizational redesign; concentration depends on whether chips, electricity, grid access, cloud, proprietary data and distribution remain scale-constrained.
signal_rationale.transmission: The shift transmits through entry-level hiring, apprenticeship structures, software pricing and valuation, capital allocation, electricity systems, cloud dependence, bargaining power and international distribution of technology rents.
signal_rationale.falsifier: The thesis weakens if exposed young-worker hiring recovers while AI adoption rises, seat-based software pricing remains dominant in agentic workflows, generic application margins retain durable premiums, and cloud/compute/energy bottlenecks and concentration fall materially.
